title_options: Apps that make you breathe before opening Instagram, compared
Breathe before Instagram: one sec, ScreenZen, Clearspace, Opal and free iPhone options compared
iPhone apps that add a breath or pause before Instagram, compared
search_intent: Commercial investigation with a how-to side. Searchers want the names of iPhone apps that put a breath or pause in front of Instagram, how each one works, what it costs and whether there's a free option. Many also want to know if Google's Pause Point works on iPhone. Format: a neutral roundup with a summary table, per-app sections and an if-then picker.
serp_summary: Results are a mix of App Store listings (one sec in several countries, plus small apps like Focus Pause, Welligama, Always Pause and BreathPause), first-person 'I tried it' pieces (TechRadar, Gizmodo AU) that lean on addiction language, aggregator pages (Product Hunt, apptail, appgoblin) and brand-run 'alternative' blogs (habitdoom, cursedscreen, TaskGate, lifestack, nibble) that rank their own product first with little or no disclosure. Pause Point queries return TechCrunch, TechRadar, Smartprix, PhoneArena and one sec's own promotional post. No result is a neutral, disclosed, structured comparison. Prices on third-party sites contradict each other, and popular write-ups blur what the one sec PNAS study actually measured.
gaps: No neutral, disclosed roundup with one row per app comparing how the pause works, whether it uses breathing, how strict it is, the free tier, the US price and the minimum iOS version, all checked against App Store listings (November 2026).
No result separates catching the reflex tap at the open from how you feel 15-20 minutes into a session.
Coverage of the PNAS study is loose. It measured opening attempts, openings, self-reported time and satisfaction, not momentary mood or stress during or after sessions.
Nobody says plainly that Opal's listing doesn't mention breathing. It is a blocker with adjustable strictness (Focus Difficulty, Waiting Room resistance, Deep Focus).

The mid-session features of one sec (Re-Intervention, the 'Doom Scroll Emergency Brake') and ScreenZen (Interrupt scrolling check-ins) are rarely described accurately. They are time-based and push you out of the app; they are not calming tools.
The Pause Point on iPhone answer either comes from one sec's own promotional post or never gets to iPhone options at all.
None of them gives a free, practical breathing script readers can use right now before or during an Instagram session.
No result uses respectful, non-addiction framing.

outline.h2: Quick answer: which apps make you breathe before opening Instagram?
points: 40-60 word answer: one sec and Clearspace show a breathing pause before Instagram opens. ScreenZen adds a delay that can grow with each open and offers breathing while you wait. Opal is a blocker with adjustable strictness. Apple's Screen Time and Shortcuts are the free built-in option but have no breathing pause.
Disclosure within the first 100 words: DeRot makes an app in this category. We don't rank our own app, and no app paid to be included.
Summary table with no DeRot row. Columns: App | Best for | How the pause works | Breathing-based? | Free option | US price (as listed) | Minimum iOS.
Note: facts come from each app's US App Store listing, checked November 2026.

outline.h2: How we compared these pause apps
points: Criteria: how it intervenes (delay, breath, block), whether breathing is built in, how strict it is and how easy it is to bypass, cost and free tier, platform and minimum iOS.
Sources: App Store listings only. No official ScreenZen, Clearspace or Opal websites were found, so nothing beyond the listings is assumed.
No invented testing, ratings or review counts.
Use the same fields for each app in the same order: Best for, How it works, What stands out, Drawbacks, Price.

### one sec: a deep-breath animation before the app opens, set up through a Shortcuts automation. The listing says it 'delays access instead of blocking.' Exercises include box, 4-7-8, Follow the Dot, math and journaling. Re-Intervention sends you out after a set time (the listing's example is 5 minutes). One app free. Pro $6.99/mo, $19.99/yr, $99.99 lifetime. iOS 15.0+, plus Mac.

### ScreenZen: a delay that can increase each time, 'Is this important' messages, Interrupt scrolling check-ins, breathing and other activities while you wait, Practice mode, and strict blocking with a settings lock. Free, funded by tips ($5-$40). iOS 16.4+.

### Clearspace: 'proceed after a breath or opt out', described as a reminder to breathe before making decisions. The listing doesn't state the pause length. Premium $6.99/mo or $44.99/yr, Family $79.99. iOS 16.0+.

### Opal: scheduled blocking, a Waiting Room with Standard or Increasing resistance, user-set unblock waits, and Deep Focus, which can't be bypassed. The listing doesn't mention breathing. A fair pick for people who want firmness. Many price tiers are listed, including $99.99/yr. iOS 18.0+, iPhone only.

### Apple Screen Time and Shortcuts (free): App Limits with 'Ignore Limit' unless 'Block at End of Limit' is on. A Shortcuts 'App is opened' automation can run an action such as starting a Focus. No built-in breathing pause. Describe these in general terms only.

outline.h2: Do pause-before-opening apps actually work? What the research shows
points: The PNAS one sec field study (719 users, 280 completed 6 weeks): 36% of open attempts were dismissed, attempts fell 37% and actual openings fell 57%.
In the online experiment (N=500), the option to dismiss had the strongest effect, the delay also helped, and the message did not.
Limits: users self-selected, the field study had no control group, dropout may bias results, and one author made the app.
The study measured opens and satisfaction, not mood or stress during or after sessions. It supports friction at the open and says little about the comedown.

outline.h2: A pause at the open vs. how you feel 20 minutes in
points: A pause catches the reflex tap. It doesn't help much once you're 15 minutes in and wound up.
Be fair: one sec's Re-Intervention and ScreenZen's Interrupt scrolling do act mid-session, but they are time-based and push you out of the app. They aren't built to calm you down.
Mid-scroll moment: the jaw is clenched, you feel wired, and that's the point to use a breath.

outline.h2: Is there Google Pause Point for iPhone?
points: Pause Point is an Android feature (Android 17, per TechCrunch): a 10-second pause on apps you've labelled distracting, with a breathing option, and turning it off needs a restart.
It isn't on iPhone. Sources disagree on exactly which Android devices get it, so the article should say only 'Android, not iPhone.'
On iPhone, the closest options are the apps above plus Screen Time App Limits and a Shortcuts 'App is opened' automation. Don't speculate about iOS 27.

outline.h2: A 30-second Calm 4-6 breath for Instagram, before or mid-scroll
points: Script: put the phone face down or keep your thumb still. Inhale through the nose for 4, exhale slowly for 6. Repeat 3 times (about 30 seconds). Notice your shoulders and jaw.
Use it at the open, or when you notice the wired feeling partway through a session.
Link to the free calm 4-6 breathing tool at /tools/.

Evidence, kept proportional: Balban 2023 found exhale-focused cyclic sighing gave the largest daily gain in positive affect in a 5-minute-a-day RCT of 108 people. That was not a 30-second practice. The Fincham meta-analysis found a small-to-moderate effect on stress and asks for cautious interpretation.
Safety: breathe gently and stop if you feel dizzy.
If you want a breathing animation at the open with the option to go in anyway, pick one sec (one app free).
If you want it free with escalating delays and a lot of options, pick ScreenZen.
If you want a simple 'breathe or opt out' prompt, pick Clearspace.
If you want a firm block that's hard to bypass, pick Opal.
If you want to pay nothing and install nothing, use Screen Time App Limits or a Shortcuts automation, knowing neither includes a breath.
Short and clearly labeled. Not ranked.
It meets you mid-scroll, for people who don't mind opening Instagram but don't like how they feel 20 minutes later.
DeRot pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths (Calm 4-6 by default).
Pre-launch: coming soon to iOS, with a launch newsletter.
Who it's not for: people who want a hard lockout or a gate at the open.

research_notes:
# Research notes: "app that makes you breathe before opening instagram" (roundup)

I checked everything on 2026-11-10. I used all 10 searches, plus page fetches of the US App Store listings, the one sec PNAS paper, the Balban 2023 paper, TechCrunch on Pause Point and one sec's own Pause Point post.

Before you write, there are three problems:
- **No official websites for ScreenZen, Clearspace or Opal.** Their sites never came up in search. Opal's only link redirected to an address that wasn't in the results, so I didn't use it. App facts below come from the App Store listings only. The page should say so: "facts from each app's App Store listing, checked November 2026."
- **No official Apple support page** for Screen Time or Shortcuts came up. I only have Apple Community threads and How-To Geek, so describe Apple's tools in general terms.
- **The timing angle needs softening.** one sec and ScreenZen both say in their listings that they also step in during a session, not only at the open. Details are in GAPS AND ANGLE.

## SERP ANALYSIS

**What ranks:**
- **App Store listings.** one sec shows up in several countries, plus small apps: Focus Pause, MindPause, Welligama "Breathe to Unlock", Always Pause, BreathPause.
- **First-person "I tried it" articles.** TechRadar's "I was addicted to Instagram…" uses one sec's free tier with Instagram. The page body didn't load, so this comes from the search snippet. Gizmodo AU's "might actually help you break your social media addiction" is also first-person.
- **App aggregator pages.** Product Hunt, apptail, appgoblin.
- **Brand-run "alternative" blogs.** These are competitor marketing: habitdoom.com (on ScreenZen and Clearspace), cursedscreen and the TaskGate pages (on Opal), lifestack and nibble on ScreenZen.

**Format:** There is no neutral, structured roundup. Results are single-app reviews, App Store pages, or competitor blogs that put their own product first.

**"Google Pause Point iPhone" results:**
- TechCrunch, 12 May 2026.
- TechRadar, comparing iOS 27 Screen Time with Android 17's Pause Point.
- Smartprix, Stuff.tv (blocked when I tried to open it), PhoneArena.
- one sec's own post "Pause Point for iPhone? Here's the Alternative for iOS: one sec" (24 Aug 2026).

The one sec post recommends only one sec. It doesn't say outright that the maker wrote it; that's only implied by the "our goal" wording and the domain.

**What they do well:** Clear setup steps for one sec via the Shortcuts automation, and the free-tier detail (one app free).

**What they miss or get wrong:**
- Nearly all of them use addiction language.
- None compares how strict each app is or what it costs side by side.
- None separates the pause at the open from how you feel after a session.
- Competitor blogs don't disclose, or barely disclose.
- Prices quoted on third-party sites contradict each other. Opal is quoted at $59.99, $99.99 or $19.99/mo depending on the site; Clearspace at "$6.99 mo" from a rival's blog.
- Popular write-ups blur what the PNAS study actually measured.

## GAPS AND ANGLE

1. **Neutral, disclosed roundup with one row per app.** Columns: how the pause works, whether it's breathing-based, how strict it is, free tier, US price, minimum iOS. All of it can be checked against the listings.
2. **Opal is not a breathing-pause app according to its own listing.** The listing doesn't mention breathing at all. Its gentler options are "Focus Difficulty: make it hard, or make it a bit easier," a Waiting Room with Standard or Increasing "Resistance," and user-set unblock waits. Deep Focus "cannot bypass or cancel." Describe it as a blocker with adjustable strictness. It's a fair pick for people who want firmness.
3. **Timing angle: what the evidence covers.** The PNAS study measured opening attempts, openings, self-reported time and "happiness with consumption" before and after. The fetch summary says it reported **no momentary mood or stress measures** during or after sessions. So it supports friction at the open and says nothing about the comedown.
4. **Timing angle: be accurate about the competitors.**
   - one sec has a "Doom Scroll Emergency Brake" (Re-Intervention): after a set time (the listing's example is 5 minutes) you're sent out of the app and have to do another intervention.
   - ScreenZen lists "Interrupt scrolling: short, timed check-ins on distracting apps."

   So don't claim the others only act at the open. The fair line is that their mid-session tools are time-based limits that push you out. DeRot's point of view is the comedown: how you feel 20 minutes in, with a calming breath rather than a timer.
5. **Pause Point on iPhone.** It's an Android 17 feature: a 10-second pause on apps you've labelled distracting, with a breathing option, and turning it off needs a restart (TechCrunch). Sources disagree on which devices get it (TechCrunch says Android 17 broadly; one sec's blog says Pixel 11 only), so just say "Android, not iPhone." For iPhone, list the apps covered here plus Screen Time App Limits and a Shortcuts "App is opened" automation. Don't speculate about iOS 27. The TechRadar iOS 27 "Time Allowances" claim came only from a search snippet and is unverified.
6. **30-second Instagram script.** Calm 4-6 is about 3 breaths of 10 seconds. Send readers to /tools/ for the calm 4-6 timer. For evidence, Balban 2023 supports exhale-focused breathing. Keep the claim proportional: a small RCT of a 5-minute daily practice, not a 30-second one.

**Things to note in the roundup:**
- one sec's listing names box breathing and 4-7-8 among its exercises, alongside math, journaling and rotating the phone.
- ScreenZen pays for itself with tips, and its wait can get longer with each open.
- Clearspace's listing says only that you "proceed after a breath or opt out"; it gives no length for the pause.

## SAFETY

- **Calm 4-6 and other slow breathing:** Breathe gently; don't force deep breaths. Stop if you feel dizzy or lightheaded, tingly or short of breath, and go back to normal breathing.
- **Box and 4-7-8 (which one sec lists):** These include breath holds. They're not for everyone, including people who are pregnant, have heart or lung conditions, or have a history of fainting or panic. The Fincham meta-analysis says fast breathwork in particular needs more safety research.
- **Unwanted effects:** About 10% of Balban participants reported negative experiences. Give readers permission to stop.
- **Claims:** Breathing may help you feel calmer. Never say it treats anxiety or anything else. Both breathing studies are small or moderate in quality.
- **Help:** Talk to a professional about persistent anxiety, sleep problems or distress. If someone is in crisis, point to local emergency services or 988 in the US.
- **Pause apps:** The one sec study shows less opening, not better mental health. Don't claim these apps improve wellbeing.
